question: In this plant cell, the large pale-blue oval is the
imageAlt: Plant cell with a thick wall, a round nucleus, small green chloroplasts, and a large pale-blue oval.
explanation: The central vacuole is the big water-filled sac. The round green body with a dark center is the nucleus. The small green ovals are chloroplasts. The thick border is the cell wall.

question: Select ALL structures you can see in this drawing.
imageAlt: Plant cell with a thick wall, a round nucleus, small green chloroplasts, and a large pale-blue oval.
explanation: The thick border is the cell wall, the small green ovals are chloroplasts, and the large pale oval is the central vacuole. Centrioles are an animal-cell structure and are not drawn here.

question: Which drawing shows a fibrous root system?
imageAlt: Two root systems under a soil-surface line. The left has one thick root with side branches. The right has many similar roots.
options: The left drawing, with one thick main root
The right drawing, with many similar roots
answer: The right drawing, with many similar roots
explanation: A fibrous system is a cluster of roots of similar size, common in grasses. The left drawing is a taproot: one main root with smaller branches.

question: The left-hand root system, with one thick main root, is the kind a carrot or dandelion uses to store food.
imageAlt: Two root systems under a soil-surface line. The left has one thick root with side branches. The right has many similar roots.
explanation: That left drawing is a taproot. Carrots and dandelions store food in a thick main root. Grasses use the fibrous system on the right.

question: Which stem cross section is typical of a monocot such as corn?
imageAlt: Two stem cross sections. The left has vascular bundles in a ring. The right has bundles scattered through the stem.
options: The left circle, with bundles in a ring
The right circle, with bundles scattered through the stem
answer: The right circle, with bundles scattered through the stem
explanation: Monocot stems usually have vascular bundles scattered in the ground tissue. Many dicot stems have the bundles in a ring, like the left circle.

question: The left-hand circle has vascular bundles arranged in a ring. That pattern is typical of which major flowering-plant group?
imageAlt: Two stem cross sections. The left has vascular bundles in a ring. The right has bundles scattered through the stem.
explanation: A ring of bundles is the usual dicot (eudicot) stem pattern. The scattered pattern on the right is typical of monocots.

question: The tall, tightly packed cells just under the upper surface are
imageAlt: Leaf cross section with a top layer, a row of tall dark cells, a layer of round cells, and a small pore on the lower surface.
explanation: Palisade cells stand in columns under the upper epidermis and hold many chloroplasts. The rounder cells below them are spongy mesophyll, with air spaces. The small opening on the lower surface is a stoma.

question: Name the small opening in the lower surface of this leaf.
imageAlt: Leaf cross section with a top layer, a row of tall dark cells, a layer of round cells, and a small pore on the lower surface.
explanation: A stoma is a pore between guard cells. Open stomata let carbon dioxide in and water vapor out.

question: The orange clusters on these leaflets are
imageAlt: A fern frond with green leaflets and many small orange clusters.
explanation: A sorus (plural sori) is a cluster of sporangia, usually on the underside of a fern leaflet. Spores form there. Ferns do not make seeds.

question: The plant in this drawing reproduces with seeds enclosed in fruit.
imageAlt: A fern frond with green leaflets and many small orange clusters.
explanation: The orange clusters are sori, where ferns make spores. Seeds enclosed in fruit are an angiosperm feature.

question: The large orange parts of this flower are the
imageAlt: A flower with orange petals, green sepals, pale stamens, and a green pistil in the center.
explanation: Petals are often the showy parts that attract pollinators. The smaller green parts at the base are sepals. The center holds the stamens and the pistil.

question: The green structure in the very center, with a dark tip, is the female part of the flower. What is it called?
imageAlt: A flower with orange petals, green sepals, pale stamens, and a green pistil in the center.
explanation: The pistil (made of one or more carpels) has a stigma at the tip, a style, and an ovary. The pale structures around it are stamens, which make pollen.

question: The orange region at the tip, opposite the growth arrow, is the
imageAlt: A root tip colored in bands, with an orange tip and an arrow marked growth direction.
explanation: The root cap covers the tip and protects the dividing cells as the root pushes through soil. Growth continues back from that tip, in the direction of the arrow.

question: The darkest green band just above the orange tip is where most new root cells are produced. That band is the
imageAlt: A root tip colored in bands, with an orange tip and an arrow marked growth direction.
explanation: The apical meristem, in the zone of cell division, sits just behind the root cap. Cells lengthen in the zone of elongation. Root hairs appear farther up, in the zone of maturation.

question: In this diagram, water moves from the roots up to the leaves in the
imageAlt: A plant column with leaves at the top and roots at the bottom. A blue pipeline is labeled xylem, water up. An orange pipeline is labeled phloem, sugar down.
explanation: Xylem carries water and dissolved minerals upward. Phloem carries sugar from the leaves toward the rest of the plant, including the roots.

question: The main pull that draws water up the blue pipeline is
imageAlt: A plant column with leaves at the top and roots at the bottom. A blue pipeline is labeled xylem, water up. An orange pipeline is labeled phloem, sugar down.
options: the root cap pushing soil aside
explanation: Water evaporates from leaves through stomata. That transpiration pull, plus water molecules sticking together, draws the water column up the xylem.

question: Which drawing lets carbon dioxide into the leaf?
imageAlt: Two pairs of guard cells. The left pair is closed. The right pair is open, with carbon dioxide going in and oxygen plus water going out.
explanation: When guard cells bend apart, the pore opens. Carbon dioxide can enter for photosynthesis, and water vapor can leave.

question: A plant is most likely to use the closed pair when it needs to
imageAlt: Two pairs of guard cells. The left pair is closed. The right pair is open, with carbon dioxide going in and oxygen plus water going out.
explanation: Closing stomata cuts the path for water vapor. The tradeoff is that less carbon dioxide can enter, so photosynthesis slows.

question: Select ALL substances this diagram shows leaving the chloroplast.
imageAlt: A chloroplast with light, carbon dioxide, and water going in, and oxygen and sugar coming out.
explanation: Light, carbon dioxide, and water go in. Photosynthesis stores energy in sugar and releases oxygen.

question: Which group on this line encloses its seeds in a fruit?
imageAlt: Four groups in a row: bryophyte, fern, gymnosperm, and angiosperm, with a note that seed and water independence increase toward the right.
explanation: Angiosperms are the flowering plants. Their seeds develop inside a fruit. Gymnosperms have seeds, but the seeds are not enclosed in a fruit. Bryophytes and ferns use spores.

question: Select ALL groups on this line whose sperm must swim through water to reach the egg.
imageAlt: Four groups in a row: bryophyte, fern, gymnosperm, and angiosperm, with a note that seed and water independence increase toward the right.
explanation: Mosses and ferns still need a film of water for fertilization. Gymnosperms and angiosperms deliver sperm through a pollen tube, so they are less tied to wet conditions.

question: On this cycle, the stage that grows right after gametes fuse is the
imageAlt: A life-cycle circle: sporophyte, spores made by meiosis, gametophyte, and gametes fusing.
explanation: Fertilization joins two gametes and starts the diploid sporophyte. That sporophyte later makes haploid spores by meiosis.

question: The gametophyte is already haploid. It produces gametes by
imageAlt: A life-cycle circle: sporophyte, spores made by meiosis, gametophyte, and gametes fusing.
explanation: Meiosis happens when the sporophyte makes spores, which is why the spores are marked n. The haploid gametophyte then makes gametes by mitosis, so the chromosome number does not get cut in half again.

question: Photosynthesis moves carbon into plants from which part of this diagram?
imageAlt: A cycle linking atmosphere, plants, consumers and decomposers, and soil nutrients.
options: The plant's roots, with no carbon in the air
explanation: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and build sugars. Animals and decomposers return carbon to the air and nutrients to the soil.

question: Which circle in this diagram includes the organisms that break dead plants down and return nutrients to the soil?
imageAlt: A cycle linking atmosphere, plants, consumers and decomposers, and soil nutrients.
explanation: Decomposers, grouped here with consumers, release nutrients from dead material back into the soil. Plants then take those nutrients up again.

question: In this sequence, the stage immediately after pioneer grasses is
imageAlt: A timeline from bare ground to pioneer grasses, then shrubs, then a climax forest.
explanation: This is ecological succession. Bare ground is colonized by pioneer grasses, then shrubs, and later a taller climax forest.

question: On this diagram, the climax forest is the earliest stage.
imageAlt: A timeline from bare ground to pioneer grasses, then shrubs, then a climax forest.
explanation: Time runs from bare ground toward the climax forest. The climax community is the later, more stable stage, not the first one.

question: Older leaves are yellow while the newest growth stays green. That pattern is typical of a shortage of
imageAlt: A plant with yellow older leaves and green new growth at the bottom of the stem.
options: water only, with no mineral involved
explanation: Nitrogen is mobile. A short plant moves it out of older leaves and into new growth, so the older leaves yellow first. The drawing is a deficiency symptom, not an infectious disease.

question: Both curves dip lowest in the middle of the graph. Leaves look green mainly because chlorophyll absorbs the least light in which region?
imageAlt: Graph of absorbance versus wavelength for chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b, with a visible-light color bar.
credit: Graph: Wikimedia Commons, File:Chlorophyll_ab_spectra-en.svg, CC BY-SA 3.0.
options: Green, near the middle of the color bar
answer: Green, near the middle of the color bar
explanation: Chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b absorb strongly in the blue-violet and red, and weakly in the green. Green light is reflected or passed through, so leaves look green.

question: On the right side of the graph, which pigment reaches a high peak at the longer wavelength?
imageAlt: Graph of absorbance versus wavelength for chlorophyll a and chlorophyll b, with a visible-light color bar.
credit: Graph: Wikimedia Commons, File:Chlorophyll_ab_spectra-en.svg, CC BY-SA 3.0.
options: Both peak at the same wavelength
explanation: Chlorophyll a’s red peak sits farther right, near the long-wavelength end of red. Chlorophyll b’s red peak is a bit farther left. Both still absorb red light; they do not absorb it at exactly the same wavelength.
